title: The world held its breath (Exodus Rabbah 29:9)
hook: at Sinai no bird sang, no ox lowed, the sea was still
tomorrow: so did everyone at Sinai hear the same voice?

segments.voice: Yesterday, two tellings of Sinai: the Torah offered to all and freely chosen, and a mountain held up like a barrel. Offered to all. Now the moment itself, by ear.

Noise-canceling headphones make a strange sound when they switch on: no sound. The bus, the fan, the chatter all step back at once, and the hush is so sudden it feels like a sound of its own. For a second you can hear your own pulse. Exodus describes Sinai as loud. Thunder, lightning, a thick cloud, a shofar blast growing louder and louder. But a midrash in Exodus Rabbah listens to the next moment, the instant the words begin, and hears something else entirely.
screen: `THE HUSH WHEN THE NOISE STOPS.` → `THUNDER, CLOUD, SHOFAR.` → `THEN, THE NEXT MOMENT.`

segments.voice: Rabbi Abbahu says, in the name of Rabbi Yochanan: when God gave the Torah, no bird chirped. No bird flew. No ox lowed. Even the angels went still: the Ofanim didn't fly, the Seraphim didn't call out holy. The sea didn't stir. No creature spoke. The whole world was silent and hushed, and the voice went out: "I am the LORD thy God." In Hebrew the first word is Anokhi, I. Listen to how the list moves: a sparrow, a farm animal, the angels, the ocean, every living thing. Small to huge, near to far, until nothing in creation is making a sound. And notice what the list leaves out: nobody tells the people to be quiet. No one shushes anyone. The stillness simply arrives, and they are standing inside it. That's the thing to tell a friend tonight: in this midrash, the loudest moment in the Torah's story is also the quietest. The thunder is outside. The words come into a world that has stopped to listen. The midrash doesn't spell out why, and it doesn't need to. Anyone who has tried to say something that matters in a room full of noise knows what it's after. Big words need a still place to land. Some people stand when this passage is read in synagogue, a small way of holding still for it.
screen: `NO BIRD, NO OX, NO ANGEL.` · `SMALL TO HUGE, ALL STILL.` · `THE THUNDER IS OUTSIDE.` · `BIG WORDS NEED A STILL PLACE.` · then, large: `THE WORLD HELD ITS BREATH.`

segments.voice: Set your phone face down and keep your eyes open, wherever you are. For one minute, listen for the quietest sound around you: a fridge humming, a car far off, your own breath. Then let even that slide into the background, and stay with the stillness that's left until the bell.
screen: `PHONE DOWN, EYES OPEN.` · `THE QUIETEST SOUND.` · `THEN, THE STILLNESS.`

segments.voice: The world held its breath: Exodus Rabbah's picture of Sinai. No bird, no ox, no sea, no angel, and into that stillness, one voice.
screen: `THE WORLD HELD ITS BREATH — today's word`.

segments.voice: Hold onto this: the world held its breath. The thunder was outside; the words came into the quiet.

howItsDone: In synagogue the Ten Commandments are read aloud from the Torah scroll several times a year, including on Shavuot; in some congregations people stand while they are read.

notes: Exodus Rabbah 29:9 paraphrased; confirm the list (bird did not chirp, fowl did not fly, ox did not low, Ofanim did not fly, Seraphim did not say Kadosh, the sea did not stir, creatures did not speak) and the attribution to Rabbi Abbahu in the name of Rabbi Yochanan.

The midrash continues with a comparison to Elijah at Carmel (an explanation of the silence); the lesson says 'the midrash doesn't spell out why' about the list itself. A Keeper may prefer to mention the Elijah passage or soften that line. Please check.

'Some people stand when this passage is read in synagogue' and howItsDone 'in some congregations people stand': a known custom, debated in halakhic sources (Maimonides discouraged it). Confirm phrasing.
Exodus 20:2 quoted from JPS 1917 ('I am the LORD thy God'); confirm.
'The loudest moment… also the quietest' is the lesson's own framing of Exodus 19 against the midrash; not a superlative claim from a source. Confirm a Keeper is comfortable.
Gloss: Ofanim from Ezekiel's vision (Ezekiel 1), Seraphim from Isaiah 6. Confirm.
